source_document.body:
Air cargo is heading into peak season with a familiar mix of good news and bad. Global demand was up 6% year over year in October, according to Xeneta , and spot rates averaged $3.11 per kilogram . FreightWaves puts rates up about 30% year over year . On paper, that looks like a strong market. On the ramp, in the warehouse and at the booking desk, it looks like something else: a system straining to move more freight through capacity that rarely sits where shippers need it.
The question for airlines, forwarders and shippers isn’t whether these pressures will ease. Some will, some won’t. The real question is which of them are structural, and which are the cost of running a modern, data-heavy business on technology built for a slower era.
The good news is that a new generation of cloud-native, AI-driven cargo platforms is turning each of these pressures into something carriers can manage, and in many cases monetize.
Capacity is there. It’s just in the wrong place.
Freighter additions remain limited, and passenger belly capacity follows passenger demand, not cargo demand. IATA data show August volumes from Asia to North America up 15% year over year, while Asia–Europe fell 8%. The pressure is concentrated on routes from Vietnam, Thailand and Taiwan to the U.S., while other corridors fly with room to spare.
Airlines can’t reposition aircraft to chase every surge. But they can get far better at seeing and selling the space they already fly. Many carriers still plan cargo capacity against static assumptions: a standard allotment per aircraft type, adjusted by hand when passenger loads or fuel change. AI changes that math. Machine learning models trained on historical flown cargo, passenger and baggage loads, aircraft configuration, fuel and seasonal patterns can predict available belly space flight by flight, days before departure, and refresh that prediction as bookings and passenger counts move. Carriers can release space earlier and with more confidence, and, in general, AI-tuned overbooking lets them sell closer to true capacity without risking offloads. Space that used to fly empty because nobody trusted the forecast becomes sellable inventory.
That’s new revenue with no new aircraft. In a market this tight, it may be the cheapest capacity an airline can add.
Rates are high. Pricing discipline is low.
Elevated spot rates are partly a symptom of disruption elsewhere. Ocean disruptions are among the forces lifting air rates , and container reliability problems keep pushing shippers into emergency airfreight, usually at the last minute and at premium cost. For carriers, that sounds like a windfall. In practice, many still price spot requests through email, spreadsheets and gut feel, approving or rejecting quotes without a clear view of how the flight is actually booking.
AI-powered dynamic pricing gives revenue teams a better answer. Models that read demand curves, booking pace and market rates can recommend a hurdle rate for each flight from two weeks out to departure, and flag which spot requests to accept, counter or decline. Decisions that once took hours of back-and-forth take minutes, and they stay consistent across stations. Carriers capture yield on the flights that will fill and stay competitive on the ones that won’t. Shippers get quicker quotes and fewer surprises. Everyone spends less time negotiating by inbox.
Compliance is now a per-parcel cost
The regulatory picture keeps getting more complicated. Tighter security protocols, shifting tariffs and new advance data requirements are landing at the same time as the end of de minimis exemptions. The U.S. suspended its $800 threshold for all countries on Aug. 29, 2025 , and the EU’s €150 duty exemption ended on July 1, 2026 . Every low-value parcel that once moved duty-free now needs accurate, piece-level data.
This is where legacy cargo systems struggle most. They were built around master air waybills and consolidated freight, not millions of individual orders each carrying its own customs record. Platforms designed around piece-level tracking capture that data once, at booking, and carry it through acceptance, screening, customs and delivery. AI adds another layer of protection, flagging vague descriptions, likely misclassified goods and unusual shipper patterns before a parcel reaches the screening line. Compliance stops being a manual reconciliation exercise and becomes a byproduct of the shipment record.
Fuel and margin pressure punish inefficiency
High and volatile fuel costs keep squeezing carrier margins, and the casualties are mounting. According to IATA fuel prices have had a CAGR of 127.46% for U.S. commercial airline fuel from February to September 2026.
AI-driven load optimization is a quiet lever here. Algorithms that build Unit Load Devices (ULDs) in three dimensions around actual shipment dimensions and weight, rather than a planner’s last-minute best guess, fit more revenue cargo on each departure and cut the offloads that turn into rebooking costs and unhappy customers. Integrated dashboards that put AI forecasts of capacity, revenue and cost side by side let teams spot unprofitable flights before they depart, not after the month closes.
Hubs are congested. Data shouldn’t be.
Runway congestion, overbooked warehouse space, understaffed ground handling teams and paperwork backlogs all slow cargo at major airports. Technology won’t add runways. It can remove much of the friction around them.
Cloud-based cargo platforms with open APIs let forwarders book and track through a single integration instead of juggling carrier portals. Electronic air waybills and real-time status updates cut the phone calls and re-keying that eat handler time, and AI document capture can read the paperwork that still arrives on paper. AI-driven exception alerts for a missed connection, a screening hold or a capacity change surface problems while there’s still time to fix them. And because modern platforms deploy in weeks rather than the 18 to 24 months typical of legacy replacements, carriers don’t have to wait years to feel the benefit.
Small parcels, big opening
The biggest opportunity may be the one legacy cargo systems were never built to see: small-parcel e-commerce. Shoppers now expect next-day or two-day delivery, and ground networks struggle to deliver it coast to coast. Passenger airlines already fly thousands of domestic departures a day with belly space to spare. Connect that capacity to e-commerce shippers, and every passenger flight becomes a parcel route, with no new aircraft required.
The demand is there. E-commerce is driving Asia–Latin America air volumes, which rose 23% year over year in August, according to IATA .
Capturing it takes parcel-native technology: online booking, piece-level tracking from booking to doorstep, API connections to retailers and last-mile partners, and AI that predicts which flights will have room for parcels tomorrow. Carriers that get there can launch a parcel product in weeks, earn revenue on space that would otherwise fly empty, and compete for a share of a delivery market that ground carriers have long owned.
The opportunity hiding in the squeeze
Every pressure on this list raises the cost of doing air cargo the old way. Customers and prospects reward carriers that can see their capacity clearly, price it intelligently, comply automatically and move freight without friction. In cargo, AI is moving out of the pilot phase and becoming the operating layer that makes all of that possible.
The airlines that come out of this cycle stronger won’t necessarily be the ones with the most freighters. They’ll be the ones that treat every passenger flight as a cargo opportunity, and run it on cloud-native, AI-driven technology built for the market they’re actually in.
About SmartKargo
SmartKargo is the AI-powered, cloud-based platform that turns airlines into world-class cargo carriers, with cargo management, e-commerce, and AI in one system. Our cargo ERP runs the entire shipment lifecycle, from booking and acceptance to handling, tracking, and last-mile delivery. Our e-commerce solutions let airlines launch parcel products in weeks and connect directly to online retailers. Our AI applications forecast capacity and demand, guide pricing, and optimize load plans, so airlines capture revenue that legacy systems leave on the table. Trusted by airlines across North America, Latin America, India, and beyond, SmartKargo is making every flight a cargo opportunity. SmartKargo is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, with key offices in India, the Philippines, Brazil, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and Canada.
